title: Oil & Gas Field Services in the US
one_liner: A volatile, highly specialized contractor market tied to drilling, completions, production maintenance, rig activity, oil prices and natural gas demand.
overview: The industry is a fee-for-service and contract-services market serving upstream oil and gas operators rather than owning most reserves itself. Baseline 2022 revenue was $82.2 billion after a 2020 collapse and 2021–2022 rebound. By 2025, the market remained below the 2022 drilling-activity peak in rig terms, but US crude production reached 13.6 million barrels per day in 2025 and EIA forecast 13.8 million barrels per day in 2026, keeping completion, production-support, artificial-lift and well-intervention work active. The 2025 US rotary rig average was 561 versus 599 in 2024 and 723 in 2022, so service intensity, pricing, efficiency and production-maintenance work matter more than simple rig-count growth. In 2026, higher oil prices and stronger gas/LNG fundamentals improved the tone, but customers are still prioritizing cash returns, productivity and lower-cost well designs.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated US industry revenue of about $80 billion-$84 billion, benchmarked to the 2022 IBISWorld baseline of $82.2 billion and updated with 2025 rig-count and major-company North America results.
key_stats.growth: 2025 estimated flat to low-single-digit decline versus 2024; 2026 expected low-single-digit growth as EIA forecast US crude production rising to 13.8 million barrels per day in 2026 and Baker Hughes showed US rigs at 587 on July 24, 2026, up 45 year over year.
key_stats.rig_count: 2025 US rotary rigs averaged 561, down 6.3% from 599 in 2024; oil rigs averaged 442 in 2025 and gas rigs averaged 113 in 2025.
key_stats.production: EIA July 2026 STEO forecast US crude production at 13.6 million barrels per day in 2025, 13.8 million barrels per day in 2026 and 14.0 million barrels per day in 2027.
key_stats.prices: EIA July 2026 STEO listed Brent crude at $69 per barrel in 2025 and $82 per barrel in 2026; Henry Hub natural gas at $3.53 per MMBtu in 2025 and $3.67 per MMBtu in 2026.
key_stats.employment: BLS reported Support Activities for Mining employment of 263,700 in June 2026 and 2025 occupational employment of 34,600 roustabouts, 29,090 service unit operators, 9,360 rotary drill operators and 8,940 derrick operators.
key_stats.geography: 2025–2026 activity remains concentrated in Texas, Oklahoma, Louisiana, New Mexico, North Dakota, Colorado, Pennsylvania, Wyoming and offshore Gulf of America work.

baseline_2022.growth: 2022 revenue increased 7.0% in 2022 but declined at a 3.9% CAGR over 2017–2022.
baseline_2022.profit: 2022 profit of $6.579 billion and 2022 profit margin of 8.0%.
baseline_2022.employment: 2022 employment of 317,799 workers and 2022 wages of $22.919 billion.
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022 revenue mix: oilfield support services 44.2%, oil drilling services 32.9%, natural gas well support services 11.2%, natural gas drilling services 8.3%, coal mining support 1.1%, metallic ore mining support 1.4%.

how_it_makes_money: Companies earn revenue from day-rate, footage-rate, turnkey, rental, product-and-service and project contracts for drilling, completions, pressure pumping, cementing, wireline, casing, well logging, well testing, coiled tubing, artificial lift, workover, production chemicals, subsea systems and field-equipment support. Pricing power rises when rigs, completion crews and specialized equipment are scarce, and falls quickly when producers reduce drilling budgets.
cost_structure: Major costs are skilled field labor, pressure-pumping and drilling equipment, fuel, steel-intensive consumables, maintenance, logistics, insurance, safety compliance, depreciation and technology spend. In 2022, wages were 27.9% of revenue and profit margin was 8.0%. In 2025, Halliburton held capital expenditures near 6% of revenue, Baker Hughes OFSE EBITDA margin was about 18.3% on $14.324 billion of 2025 OFSE revenue, and labor scarcity plus equipment upkeep remained margin constraints even as larger providers used automation, digital operations and fleet rationalization to protect returns.

current_dynamics: The 2025–2026 market is being pulled in two directions: US oil and gas production is at or near records, but fewer rigs and more efficient wells mean service providers are competing for a smaller number of higher-productivity projects. Producers are prioritizing capital discipline, longer laterals, pad optimization and completion efficiency. Gas-linked work improved from 2024 lows because Henry Hub prices rose to $3.53 per MMBtu in 2025 and EIA forecast $3.67 per MMBtu in 2026, while LNG export growth supports long-term gas development. Oilfield service demand is strongest where production maintenance, artificial lift, completions intensity, offshore projects and digital optimization are required, while commodity-price swings still drive sudden spending resets.
whats_growing: 2025–2026 production support, artificial lift and intervention work as shale wells require ongoing maintenance after completion.
2025–2026 natural-gas-linked services tied to LNG feedgas growth, Permian associated gas and higher Henry Hub prices versus 2024.
2026 offshore and subsea work, including Gulf of America and international offshore projects, supported by long-cycle capital programs.
2025–2026 digital operations, reservoir modeling, automation and drilling-efficiency tools, including SLB reporting 2025 digital revenue growth of 9%.
2025–2026 larger integrated providers gaining share where customers need bundled drilling, completions, chemicals, lift and data services.
whats_shrinking: 2025 US rig-linked drilling activity, with average US rotary rigs down to 561 from 599 in 2024 and 723 in 2022.
2025 oil-directed drilling, with oil rigs averaging 442 in 2025 versus 491 in 2024.
2025 North America OFSE revenue at Baker Hughes, down 5% year over year, and Halliburton 2025 North America revenue, down 6% year over year.
Lower-margin spot work for small contractors where fleets are underutilized or customers rebid aggressively.
Coal and metallic-ore support services, which were only 2.5% of the 2022 baseline mix.
recent_developments: 2025-11: EIA reported Lower 48 oil and gas rigs had fallen from 750 in December 2022 to 517 in October 2025 as prices softened and drilling efficiency improved.
2026-01: Baker Hughes reported the December 2025 average US rig count was 546, down 43 rigs year over year.
2026-02: Baker Hughes filed 2025 results showing OFSE revenue of $14.324 billion in 2025, down 8% from 2024, including North America OFSE revenue down 5%.
2026-02: Halliburton filed 2025 results showing total revenue down 3% and North America revenue down 6% in 2025.
2026-07: EIA July 2026 STEO forecast US crude production at 13.8 million barrels per day in 2026 and Henry Hub gas at $3.67 per MMBtu in 2026.
2026-07: SLB, Halliburton and Baker Hughes each reported sequential North America revenue improvement in 2026 Q2, signaling a near-term activity recovery from weaker 2025 conditions.
outlook: The 2026–2027 outlook is cautiously positive but not a broad boom. EIA forecast US crude production rising from 13.6 million barrels per day in 2025 to 13.8 million barrels per day in 2026 and 14.0 million barrels per day in 2027, while US LNG exports were forecast to rise from 15.1 Bcf/d in 2025 to 17.4 Bcf/d in 2026 and 18.6 Bcf/d in 2027. That supports completions, production equipment, workover, artificial-lift and gas-basin services. The main constraint is capital discipline: operators can grow output with fewer rigs, and service-company pricing may remain uneven unless utilization tightens. Larger integrated providers should outperform smaller contractors through scale, technology, bundled offerings and international/offshore exposure.

title: Oil & Gas Pipeline Construction in the US
one_liner: Pipeline contractors are benefiting from record U.S. hydrocarbon output, LNG export buildout and Gulf Coast gas bottlenecks, but permitting risk, steel costs and oil-price cycles keep revenue volatile.
overview: The industry builds and upgrades the physical network that moves hydrocarbons from shale basins, processing plants, storage hubs and import/export terminals to refiners, utilities, LNG plants, petrochemical plants and local gas systems. The 2022 baseline described a mature, fragmented construction market with low concentration, heavy regulation, medium volatility and demand tied to oil and gas production, crude and natural gas prices, steel input costs, export infrastructure and aging pipeline replacement. By 2025-2026, the demand mix has tilted further toward natural gas, LNG feedgas, intrastate gathering systems and Gulf Coast takeaway capacity. EIA reported record 2025 U.S. crude oil production of 13.6 million barrels per day and record 2025 dry natural gas production of 39 trillion cubic feet, while 2025 completed natural gas pipeline projects added about 6.3 Bcf/d of capacity, mostly into the South Central/Gulf Coast region. New construction is strongest where production and export demand create bottlenecks, while maintenance, integrity and replacement work remain a steadier base because the U.S. pipeline network is already about 3.3 million miles.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 U.S. oil and gas pipeline construction market estimated at $56.4 billion by P&S Intelligence; April 2025 IBISWorld reseller summary reported industry revenue of $51.5 billion after a five-year decline.

key_stats.network_scale: 2025 PHMSA data showed 413,330 miles of natural gas transmission and gathering pipe and 227,457 miles of hazardous liquid or CO2 pipe; CRS described the broader onshore U.S. energy pipeline network as 3.3 million miles in 2025 reporting.
key_stats.production_backdrop: 2025 U.S. crude oil output reached 13.6 million barrels per day and 2025 dry natural gas output reached 39 trillion cubic feet, both records according to EIA.
key_stats.exports_backdrop: 2026 U.S. natural gas net exports forecast at 18.7 Bcf/d, up 18% from 2025, with LNG exports averaging 17.0 Bcf/d in 2026, according to EIA.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2021 revenue of $45.6 billion in 2021 dollars in the June 27, 2022 baseline file.
baseline_2022.growth: 2016-2021 revenue CAGR of -1.8% in the 2022 baseline; 2021 revenue growth of 7.0%; 2021-2026 forecast CAGR of 3.3% to $53.8 billion.
baseline_2022.profit: 2021 profit of $2.1 billion and 2021 profit margin of 4.6% in the 2022 baseline.
baseline_2022.employment: 2021 employment of 205,132 workers in the 2022 baseline, with 2026 forecast employment of 238,734 workers.
baseline_2022.products: 2021 revenue split in the baseline was 48.6% new pipelines, 48.4% pipeline additions and alterations, and 3.0% pipeline maintenance.

how_it_makes_money: Contractors earn revenue from engineering, procurement, construction management, trenching, boring, welding, pipe laying, compressor and pump station work, terminal and tank work, integrity upgrades, maintenance and emergency repair. Projects are typically sold through fixed-price, unit-price, cost-plus, master service agreement or EPC-style contracts to midstream pipeline companies, gas utilities, oil and gas producers, LNG developers, refiners, petrochemical firms and public-sector entities. Larger contractors make money by bundling design, procurement, construction crews, specialized equipment, safety compliance and project management across multi-month or multi-year jobs.
cost_structure: Major 2025-2026 cost drivers are steel and line pipe, skilled craft labor, subcontractors, heavy equipment, right-of-way work, engineering, permitting, environmental compliance, insurance and bonding. The 2022 baseline reported 2021 wages of $16.3 billion and 2021 profit margin of 4.6%, with 2026 baseline forecast profit margin of 5.1%. Margins are pressured when steel, fuel, labor or subcontractor costs rise faster than contract escalation clauses, and they improve when contractors secure reimbursable work, long-term MSAs or higher-utilization crews on large Gulf Coast and shale-basin projects.
current_dynamics: The market is in a gas-led construction cycle rather than a broad oil-pipeline boom. EIA’s 2026 reporting shows that 2025 pipeline capacity additions were concentrated in the South Central region, with Haynesville-to-Gulf Coast gathering and LNG feedgas projects prominent. Record 2025 U.S. production supports ongoing takeaway, gathering and processing connections, but 2026 oil-price expectations are less supportive than the post-pandemic rebound because EIA’s July 2026 STEO forecast Brent at $82 per barrel for 2026 and $65 per barrel for 2027. FERC’s April 13, 2026 list shows continued approvals for interstate gas projects, including the 54.9-mile, 1.597 Bcf/d Southeast Supply Enhancement Project and the 68.9-mile, 473 MMcf/d Heartland Project. Intrastate projects remain important because many gathering and in-state Gulf Coast links avoid FERC certificate jurisdiction.
whats_growing: Natural gas transmission, gathering and LNG feedgas work is growing fastest, especially in the Gulf Coast, Haynesville, Permian and South Central corridors. 2025 projects such as Louisiana Energy Gateway, New Generation Gas Gathering, Evangeline Pass Expansion, East Lateral Xpress and Texas to Louisiana Pathway added capacity for LNG and Gulf Coast demand. Replacement, integrity, compressor station, meter station, trenchless and pipeline maintenance work is also growing because PHMSA-regulated mileage remains large and aging infrastructure needs modernization. Work connected to carbon dioxide, hydrogen and renewable natural gas is emerging but still small compared with natural gas and petroleum pipelines.
whats_shrinking: Long-haul greenfield crude oil megaprojects are a smaller share of opportunity than during earlier shale buildout waves because many core basins already have major trunkline capacity and new projects face tougher permitting, litigation and stakeholder scrutiny. Pure crude takeaway work is more exposed to 2026-2027 oil-price downside than gas work, and replacement or alteration jobs can carry lower margins than newbuild projects. Contractors tied to small, speculative upstream projects are more vulnerable if producers cut capital budgets after oil-price declines or if interest rates keep project financing expensive.
recent_developments: 2025: U.S. oil and gas pipeline construction market estimated at $56.4 billion by P&S Intelligence, with a 2025-2032 projected CAGR of 8.4%.
2025: EIA reported record U.S. crude oil production of 13.6 million barrels per day and record dry natural gas production of 39 trillion cubic feet.
2025: EIA said completed U.S. natural gas pipeline projects added about 6.3 Bcf/d of capacity, with 85% serving the South Central region.
2025-10: EIA reported Louisiana Energy Gateway and New Generation Gas Gathering were in service by October 2025, adding a combined 3.5 Bcf/d from Haynesville supply toward Gillis Hub.
2026-01: FERC listed Transcontinental Gas Pipe Line’s Southeast Supply Enhancement Project as completed on January 29, 2026, adding 54.9 miles and 1.597 Bcf/d of capacity.
2026-04: EIA forecast U.S. natural gas net exports would rise 18% in 2026 to 18.7 Bcf/d as LNG facilities ramp up.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is positive but uneven. Gas pipeline, LNG feedgas, Gulf Coast, Haynesville and Permian-adjacent work should remain active because U.S. production and exports are still expanding, and EIA expects LNG exports and pipeline exports to Mexico to grow through 2027. Maintenance, integrity, replacement and compressor upgrades should provide recurring work even if newbuild permitting slows. The main risks are lower 2027 oil prices, volatile Henry Hub prices, steel and labor inflation, project delays from permitting or litigation, and capital discipline among upstream and midstream customers. Over the next few years, contractors with diversified gas utility, pipeline integrity, LNG, industrial and energy-transition work should be less exposed than contractors dependent on new crude-oil trunklines.

title: Oil Change Services in the US
one_liner: Quick-lube operators sell routine oil changes and light preventive maintenance to a large, aging U.S. vehicle fleet, while longer oil-change intervals and EV adoption cap long-run volume growth.
overview: Industry operators change motor oil, lubricate chassis and provide light preventive maintenance such as tire rotations, wiper replacement, battery service, air filters and fluid flushes, while excluding broader mechanical, body, paint, interior and glass repair. The 2022 IBISWorld baseline put industry revenue at $9.911 billion after 6.3% growth in 2022, with oil changes generating 95.3% of revenue. Current public market estimates put the U.S. oil-change service market at $8.49 billion in 2025, with a 2025-2030 CAGR forecast of 5.9%. Demand is tied less to discretionary spending than to miles driven, vehicle age and household vehicle ownership, making the category resilient but highly competitive.

baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022: 95.3% oil changes, including 33.3% semi-synthetic, 30.5% conventional, 21.0% full synthetic, 5.7% high-mileage and 4.8% diesel oil changes

how_it_makes_money: Operators earn most revenue from bundled oil-change tickets: motor oil, oil filters and technician labor sold through quick-lube bays, drive-through formats and appointment-light service centers. Margins are improved through premium synthetic oil, high-mileage oil, cabin and engine air filters, wipers, batteries, tire rotations, transmission and coolant flushes, fleet accounts, loyalty programs and digital service reminders. Franchisors also earn royalties, product supply margin, franchise fees and advertising fund contributions.
cost_structure: Major costs are motor oil, filters and other consumables; technician wages; rent or occupancy for service bays; franchise royalties and advertising; insurance and compliance; utilities; payment processing; and local marketing. The 2022 baseline showed wages of $2.481 billion and profit of $902 million on $9.911 billion of revenue, implying a 25.0% wage share and 9.1% profit margin. Synthetic and proprietary oils raise inventory cost but also support higher ticket values; tight labor markets and technician turnover pressure store-level margins.
major_players: Valvoline Instant Oil Change / Valvoline Inc.
Jiffy Lube International / Monomoy Capital Partners
Meineke Car Care Centers / Driven Brands
Express Oil Change & Tire Engineers / Mavis
Walmart Auto Care Centers and warehouse-club competitors
current_dynamics: The strongest 2025-2026 support is the aging car parc: S&P Global Mobility reported 12.8-year average light-vehicle age and 289 million vehicles in operation in 2025, with 2015-2019 registration cohorts moving into higher-maintenance years. Lower 2025 gasoline prices helped mileage affordability, but EIA reported 2025 gasoline consumption declined by less than 1% from 2024, so volume growth is modest rather than explosive. Public chains are growing faster than the fragmented base: Valvoline reported 2,409 system-wide stores and 8.2% same-store sales growth for the quarter ended March 31, 2026, while Driven Brands reported Take 5 same-store sales growth of about 6.1%-6.2% for fiscal 2025. Consolidation is active, highlighted by Shell’s July 1, 2026 completion of the $1.3 billion Jiffy Lube sale to Monomoy.
whats_growing: Full-synthetic, high-mileage and OEM-specific oil changes; add-on light maintenance; fleet and commercial accounts; digital retention programs; drive-through stay-in-car formats; franchised quick-lube unit growth; and chain consolidation are growing. Aging internal-combustion and hybrid vehicles support recurring demand, especially as high new- and used-car prices keep vehicles in service longer.
whats_shrinking: Conventional oil-change mix, diesel light-vehicle oil changes, small independents without scale purchasing or digital retention, and purely oil-only tickets are losing relative share. Long-life synthetic oils, oil-life monitoring systems, cleaner engines and battery-electric vehicles reduce service frequency or eliminate engine-oil changes entirely for part of the fleet.
recent_developments: 2025-05-21: S&P Global Mobility reported average U.S. light-vehicle age rose to 12.8 years and vehicles in operation reached 289 million.
2025-12-01: Valvoline completed its Breeze Autocare acquisition for $638.7 million, initially adding 204 quick-lube stores before required divestitures.
2026-01-07: EIA reported 2025 regular gasoline averaged $3.10 per gallon, down $0.21 from 2024, while gasoline consumption declined by less than 1%.
2026-03-31: Valvoline ended fiscal Q2 2026 with 2,409 system-wide stores and reported 8.2% system-wide same-store sales growth.
2026-05-19: Driven Brands reported fiscal 2025 revenue up 6.3% to about $1.9 billion and Take 5 same-store sales growth of 6.1%-6.2%.
2026-07-01: Shell completed the $1.3 billion sale of Jiffy Lube International and Premium Velocity Auto to Monomoy Capital Partners.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is cautiously positive: industry revenue should rise with vehicle age, fleet size, chain unit growth and higher average tickets from synthetic oils and add-on maintenance. Volume per vehicle faces structural pressure from longer service intervals and EV adoption, but 2025 EVs were still only 7.8% of new-vehicle sales and a much smaller share of vehicles in operation, so the near-term installed base remains heavily serviceable. Margin winners will be scaled operators that secure lubricant supply, staff bays efficiently and convert oil-change visits into broader preventive-maintenance baskets. Smaller independents will remain viable in local markets but face mounting competition from chains, dealerships, retailers and warehouse clubs.
one_sentence: Oil Change Services in the US is a mature consumer-services industry supported by 2025 light-vehicle age of 12.8 years and 289 million vehicles in operation, but pressured by high price competition, more efficient engines, synthetic oils with longer service intervals and a gradually electrifying fleet.

title: Oil Drilling & Gas Extraction in the US
one_liner: A capital-intensive upstream industry riding record 2025 U.S. output while 2026 earnings remain tied to volatile crude, gas and export prices.
overview: This industry covers companies that explore for, develop and produce crude oil, natural gas, lease condensate, natural gas liquids and related hydrocarbons before refining, processing or distribution. The 2025 market is smaller than the 2022 commodity-price spike but operationally stronger: EIA reported record 2025 U.S. crude oil production of 13.6 million barrels per day, record 2025 dry natural gas production of 39 trillion cubic feet and record 2025 total U.S. energy production of 107 quadrillion Btu. The business remains mature, cyclical and highly exposed to benchmark prices, but shale productivity, Permian scale, LNG export growth and consolidation have shifted the competitive advantage toward large operators with low-cost acreage, takeaway access and strong balance sheets.

how_it_makes_money: Operators earn revenue by selling crude oil, lease condensate, natural gas and natural gas liquids under spot, index-linked and term contracts to refiners, gas processors, pipeline companies, LNG exporters, utilities, petrochemical producers and marketers. Revenue is driven mainly by 2025 and 2026 commodity price realizations, production volumes, acreage quality, reserve replacement, hedging, royalties, transport differentials and the mix between oil-weighted, gas-weighted and liquids-rich basins.

cost_structure.largest_costs: Lease operating expenses, drilling and completion capital, depletion and depreciation, gathering and transportation, royalties, production taxes, water handling, compression, power, chemicals, sand, tubular goods, and oilfield services are the largest 2025-2026 cost buckets.
cost_structure.labor: The baseline file listed $24.2 billion of wages in 2022; BLS reported May 2026 average hourly earnings of $52.58 for all oil and gas extraction employees.
cost_structure.capital_intensity: High in 2025-2026 because shale wells require continuous drilling to offset decline curves and offshore projects require multiyear upfront capital.
cost_structure.margin_sensitivity: The baseline file listed a 7.1% profit margin in 2022; 2025-2026 margins rise or fall quickly with WTI, Brent, Henry Hub, NGL prices and basin-specific takeaway differentials.
cost_structure.risk_costs: Environmental compliance, methane monitoring, plugging and abandonment, spill prevention, insurance and federal or state permitting costs remain material in 2025-2026.

major_players: Chesapeake-linked gas assets under Expand Energy
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is production-rich but price-sensitive. EIA data show record 2025 crude and gas output even though 2025 Lower 48 rig counts and drilled wells fell, highlighting efficiency gains in shale. The Permian remains the core growth basin, accounting for 48% of 2025 U.S. crude oil output and producing 6.6 million barrels per day in 2025. In 2026, the EIA July 2026 STEO forecast Brent at $82 per barrel, Henry Hub near $3.67 per MMBtu, U.S. crude output at 13.8 million barrels per day and LNG exports at 17.4 billion cubic feet per day. Consolidation is reshaping competition, with ExxonMobil-Pioneer, ConocoPhillips-Marathon Oil and Chevron-Hess increasing scale and inventory depth.
whats_growing: Permian oil and associated gas, LNG-linked gas demand, natural gas liquids, offshore Gulf projects that came online in 2025, larger public operator scale, drilling productivity, methane monitoring, water recycling and analytics-led field optimization are growing in 2025-2026.
whats_shrinking: Small standalone operators without low-cost inventory, noncore asset portfolios, marginal gas volumes in constrained basins, drilling activity where 2025 WTI and 2026 price expectations do not clear breakevens, and undeveloped acreage lacking takeaway or water infrastructure are shrinking or being rationalized in 2025-2026.
recent_developments: 2024-05-03: ExxonMobil completed its Pioneer Natural Resources acquisition, more than doubling its Permian footprint and targeting about 2.0 million oil-equivalent barrels per day of Permian production in 2027.
2024-11-22: ConocoPhillips completed its Marathon Oil acquisition and added low-cost Lower 48 inventory with expected run-rate synergies above $1.0 billion within 12 months.
2025-07-18: Chevron completed its Hess acquisition after clearing closing conditions, adding Hess assets including a 30% interest in Guyana's Stabroek Block.
2026-01-21: Enverus ranked ExxonMobil No. 1 among public U.S. onshore E&P operators at 1.95 million barrels of oil equivalent per day for 2025 gross operated production.
2026-03-31: EIA reported 2025 U.S. crude oil production rose 3% to a record 13.6 million barrels per day despite fewer rigs and fewer wells.
2026-07-07: EIA's July 2026 STEO forecast 2026 Brent at $82 per barrel, 2026 U.S. crude output at 13.8 million barrels per day and 2026 LNG exports at 17.4 billion cubic feet per day.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is constructive for volumes but mixed for revenue. EIA's July 2026 forecast implies higher 2026 Brent prices than 2025, slightly higher 2026 U.S. crude output and materially higher 2026 LNG exports, supporting cash flow for oil-weighted and gas-linked producers. The risk is that global supply growth and inventory rebuilding push prices lower into 2027, pressuring high-cost acreage and slowing drilling. The likely winners through 2026 are scaled operators with Permian inventory, low decline rates, export exposure, strong hedging and disciplined capital budgets; the likely laggards are highly levered small producers and gas producers trapped behind weak basis or infrastructure constraints.

title: Oil Field Drilling Services
one_liner: Contract drillers and oilfield service firms sell the rigs, crews, directional drilling, well-construction and completion support that upstream producers need to turn acreage into producing oil and gas wells.
overview: Operators provide drilling and related well-construction services on a fee or contract basis for oil and gas producers, including spudding, drilling, redrilling, directional drilling, casing, cementing, logging, fluids, completion support and related field services. Demand is cyclical and mainly follows crude oil and natural gas prices, producer cash flow, rig utilization, well productivity, offshore project timing and shale basin activity. The industry is fragmented below the largest public oilfield service and land-drilling companies, with pricing power strongest for high-spec rigs, integrated well-construction packages, automation, digital monitoring and crews that can reduce drilling days or improve well placement.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated U.S. industry revenue of about $65B-$67B on the IBIS-style broad oilfield drilling-services basis; 2022 Economic Census employer receipts were $18.5B for NAICS 213111 Drilling Oil and Gas Wells and $94.3B for broader NAICS 213 Support Activities for Mining.
key_stats.growth: 2025 real output for NAICS 213111 was 100.7728, down 6.8% from 2024 and down 8.7% from 2022; Baker Hughes counted 588 active U.S. rigs on 2026-08-07, up 49 rigs or about 9.1% from 2025-08-08.
key_stats.rig_count: 2026-08-07 U.S. active rigs: 588; 2026-05 monthly average rotary rigs: 553, including 417 crude oil rigs and 127 natural gas rigs.
key_stats.oil_market: EIA July 2026 STEO: Brent averaged $69/bbl in 2025, forecast at $82/bbl in 2026 and $65/bbl in 2027; U.S. crude production averaged 13.6 million b/d in 2025 and is forecast at 13.8 million b/d in 2026 and 14.0 million b/d in 2027.
key_stats.employment_and_payroll: 2022 Economic Census for NAICS 213111 reported 1,742 establishments, 52,715 employees and $5.19B in annual payroll.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 baseline estimate of about $60.8B, derived from the baseline file's 2021 revenue of $58.8B and 2021-2026 forecast CAGR of 3.4%; official 2022 Census employer receipts for the narrower NAICS 213111 category were $18.5B.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 baseline growth assumption: +3.4% year over year; Federal Reserve 2022 NAICS 213111 real output index was 110.4168, up 24.4% from 2021.

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is earned through dayrate drilling contracts, footage or performance-based contracts, directional drilling and measurement-while-drilling services, well planning, cementing, casing, fluids, logging, completion and intervention support, equipment rentals, rig technology, automation tools, maintenance and mobilization fees. Large providers also bundle field services with digital optimization, reservoir evaluation and production-system offerings.
cost_structure: Costs are dominated by skilled field labor, rig crews, payroll taxes and benefits; rig depreciation, repair and maintenance; fuel and power; steel-intensive tubulars, mud, chemicals, cement and other consumables; transportation and mobilization; insurance, safety and environmental compliance; SG&A; and interest on capital-intensive fleets. In 2022, NAICS 213111 payroll equaled about 28.1% of employer receipts, while public drillers' margins varied sharply with rig utilization, dayrates, depreciation and impairment charges.

current_dynamics: The market is being pulled in two directions. U.S. crude production is at record levels and EIA forecasts further 2026 output growth, but producer discipline and volatile crude prices have limited drilling acceleration. Public service companies reported 2025 North America softness, with Halliburton North America revenue down 6%, Baker Hughes North America OFSE revenue down 5%, Patterson-UTI Drilling Services revenue down 9.8% and Nabors U.S. Drilling revenue down 5%. By August 2026, however, Baker Hughes' weekly U.S. rig count had improved 9.1% year over year, suggesting a firmer near-term activity base than mid-2025.
whats_growing: High-spec super-spec land rigs, drilling automation, remote operations, performance-based contracts, directional drilling, measurement-while-drilling, digital well planning, gas-directed drilling tied to LNG demand, Gulf of America/offshore project work and services that cut drilling days or improve wellbore placement are growing faster than commodity crew-and-rig capacity.
whats_shrinking: Lower-spec mechanical rigs, spot-market dayrate work in oversupplied basins, weaker U.S. land completion and pressure-pumping exposure, small operators without specialized equipment, and activity tied to marginal oil acreage are under pressure when crude prices fall or producers prioritize free cash flow over growth.
recent_developments: 2025-06-10: EIA said lower crude prices and a declining rig count would affect U.S. crude production trends through 2026, with 2025 production around 13.4 million b/d in that release.
2025-12-31: Halliburton reported 2025 revenue of $22.184B, down 3% from 2024, and North America revenue of $9.066B, down 6%.
2025-12-31: Baker Hughes reported 2025 OFSE revenue of $14.324B, down 8% from 2024, with North America OFSE revenue down 5%.
2026-01-16: FRED updated the 2025 NAICS 213111 real output index to 100.7728, down from 108.1024 in 2024.
2026-07-07: EIA's July 2026 STEO forecast U.S. crude production of 13.8 million b/d in 2026 and 14.0 million b/d in 2027.
2026-08-07: Baker Hughes reported 588 active U.S. rigs, unchanged from the prior week and up 49 from 2025-08-08.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is cautiously constructive but not a broad boom. Record U.S. crude production, resilient gas demand and a higher year-over-year rig count support demand for efficient well construction, especially where service providers can prove lower drilling time, better well placement or lower total well cost. The main constraint is producer capital discipline: if Brent moves toward EIA's 2027 forecast of $65/bbl, marginal oil drilling and spot-market pricing could weaken. Consolidation, automation and international diversification should continue to favor scaled providers over small contractors.
